planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; Avalanche is an AAS-winning pure-white beet that does not bleed or stain, with sweet flavor and none of the earthy, bitter aftertaste some gardeners dislike in red beets.

directions: Direct sow seed clusters 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have their first true leaves. Avalanche is an AAS-winning beet with pure-white roots and a sweet, clean flavor without the earthy or bitter aftertaste that some gardeners and children dislike in standard red beets. Because it produces no red pigment, it does not stain hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients when cooked or pickled — a genuine kitchen convenience, particularly useful for gardeners who want to combine beets with other vegetables without turning everything pink. The greens are tender and edible as well, cooked the same way as other beet tops. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly sized roots, and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best texture; oversized roots can become woody.

common_name: Just Right Turnip (AAS-Winning Mild Non-Pithy Hybrid Turnip)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Just Right was the first true F1 hybrid turnip and stays mild and non-pithy even at a large size, unlike most turnips which turn woody and strong-flavored once they size up.

directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loose soil in full sun; Just Right was the first true F1 hybrid turnip ever introduced and remains notable for staying mild, sweet, and non-pithy even when its pure-white, flattened roots are allowed to grow to a large 5-6 inches across — most turnip varieties turn woody, hollow, or sharply pungent well before reaching that size, forcing gardeners to harvest small. This gives more flexibility in harvest timing and a bigger yield per root without sacrificing quality. The tender greens are edible as well and hold up well in the kitchen. In zone 9, grow it strictly as a fall and winter crop, since heat above the mid-70s causes turnip roots to become pithy and bitter regardless of variety; sow from late summer through early fall for a harvest running into winter.
sources: All-America Selections — Just Right Turnip winner announcement

common_name: Roxanne Radish (AAS-Winning Uniform Red Globe Radish)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Roxanne is an AAS-winning early radish bred for strong resistance to pithiness and heat stress, holding good quality longer than most globe radishes.

directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; Roxanne is an AAS-winning globe radish producing uniform, bright-red, smooth roots with crisp, mild white flesh, bred for unusually strong resistance to the pithiness and hollow centers that often develop in radishes that sit in the ground a few extra days past ideal harvest size or face a warm spell. This forgiveness makes it a good choice for gardeners who cannot harvest on the exact first day of readiness. It matures quickly, in as little as 24 days, allowing several successive plantings through a spring or fall cool season. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, fast-sizing roots, and harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across for the crispest texture.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Rivoli is an AAS-winning radish bred to grow large without becoming pithy, holding dense, crisp white flesh even at an oversized root diameter.

directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun as soon as the soil can be worked. Rivoli is an AAS-winning radish notable for growing to a substantially larger round size than most globe radishes — up to 2 inches or more across — while keeping its white flesh dense and crisp rather than turning pithy or hollow the way an oversized radish typically does, giving gardeners a bigger harvest window and more flexibility about exact pick timing. Its bright red skin and clean round shape make it visually appealing for slicing and garnishing as well as eating whole. Keep soil consistently moist for the best size and texture, and it was, at the time of its award, the first radish AAS winner in several decades — reflecting a genuinely useful improvement over standard varieties rather than just a color or shape novelty.

common_name: Geisha Garlic Chives (AAS-Winning Late-Flowering Garlic Chives)

planting.note: Sow directly 4-6 weeks before last frost or transplant established divisions in spring; Geisha is an AAS-winning garlic chive bred with wider, more vigorous leaves and a later flowering time than standard garlic chives, which reduces the unwanted self-seeding that can make common garlic chives weedy.

directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and keep soil moist; germination is similar to common chives, but Geisha produces noticeably wider, more vigorous, flat, grass-like leaves with the same mild garlic flavor as standard garlic chives. Its key improvement, and the reason for its AAS award, is delayed flowering — by blooming later in the season than common garlic chives, it produces far fewer of the seed heads responsible for the prolific, sometimes weedy self-seeding that gives standard garlic chives a reputation for spreading where unwanted. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and divide clumps every 2-3 years to prevent overcrowding and keep production vigorous. Harvest the flat leaves at any height for kitchen use; older leaves become slightly tough but remain useful cooked into dishes.
